# How an error class routes

Every failed dispatch carries one **error class**: a string such as
`http/network_error`, `acquire/unavailable`, or `abandoned`. The runtime looks
that string up in the node's `error_types` map and runs the action it finds.
This page describes the lookup. The other pages in this set describe the
classes.

## The lookup is an exact string match

The runtime reads `nodes[].error_types` as a flat map and asks it for the exact
class the failure carried. There is no pattern matching, no prefix matching,
and no fallback entry.

Three consequences a template author must plan around:

- **A bare `*` entry does nothing.** `error_types: {"*": {action: pass}}`
  registers, and then never matches, because no peer emits the class `*`. A
  node with that entry behaves exactly like a node with an empty `error_types`
  map. Registration warns — `error class "*" is not in any declared vocabulary
  … the policy registers but will only match if a peer emits this exact class`
  — and the warning does not fail the register.
- **A trailing-wildcard key such as `http/*` does nothing either.** The
  wildcard convention belongs to the *declaring* side: an executor may
  advertise `http/request_invalid/*` to say "I emit classes beneath this
  prefix", and the registration-time vocabulary check honours that when
  deciding whether to warn. Routing does not. A node that declares
  `error_types: {"http/*": {action: retry}}` and then takes an
  `http/network_error` failure has no matching entry and gives up. Even
  `http/request_invalid/*`, a family the executor itself advertises, does not
  route the concrete `http/request_invalid/<code>` class the executor emits.
- **Enumerate the classes you intend to handle.** Write
  `error_types: {"http/network_error": {action: retry}, "http/timeout":
  {action: retry}}`, one key per class you want to act on. The pages in this
  set list the literal strings each emitter produces.

The one wildcard key that matches anything is the acquire family's fallback,
and it is not a prefix rule — see [acquire.md](acquire.md).

## What happens when nothing matches

The runtime gives up: it settles the run with a **failed** color and records
the reason `unknown_error_class`. Fail-fast is the default; every other outcome
is opt-in. This is why a node that uses claim producers and declares no
`acquire/unavailable` entry fails on the first unavailable claim rather than
waiting — registration warns about exactly that case.

## The four actions

`nodes[].error_types.<class>.action` takes one of four values. Any other value
is a hard registration error naming the valid set.

| Action | What the runtime does |
| --- | --- |
| `retry` | Sleeps the backoff delay, then re-attempts the same operation in place. Claims already held stay acquired, the attribute bag is unchanged, and the dispatch id is preserved. No new run row appears; the per-dispatch retry counter advances. |
| `give_up` | Settles the run with a failed color. `nodes[].error_types.<class>.reason` supplies the recorded reason; with no reason set, the runtime records `give_up`. |
| `pass` | Settles the run with a fresh (success) color, treating the failure as benign for downstream cascade purposes. |
| `release_and_requeue` | Releases the run's acquired claim handles, clears the run's abandoned claim handles, and re-enqueues the dispatch for a fresh acquire on the next cycle. |

`pass` and `give_up` differ only in the color the run settles with; both are
terminal for that dispatch. `retry` and `release_and_requeue` both re-run the
node — `retry` keeps the claims it holds, `release_and_requeue` gives them
back first.

The map is flat and has no per-attempt chain. A class mapped to `pass` passes
every time it occurs; there is no "retry twice, then pass" spelling inside one
entry.

## The retry budget

`nodes[].max_retries` caps the number of retries **per dispatch**, counted
across every error class that occurs in that dispatch. It is unset by default,
which means unbounded retries. When the counter reaches the cap, the runtime
converts the next retry into a give-up with the reason
`max_retries_exhausted`.

The counter lives on the run and resets to zero when a new run starts for the
same node. The budget is per-dispatch, never cross-dispatch.

## The retry backoff

`nodes[].retry_backoff` shapes the delay before an in-place retry.

| Key | Values | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `kind` | `linear`, `exponential` | `linear` yields `base_delay_ms × (n+1)` on retry index `n`; `exponential` yields `base_delay_ms × 2ⁿ`. Unset yields a flat `base_delay_ms`. |
| `jitter` | `none`, `plus_minus` | `plus_minus` multiplies the computed delay by a random factor between 0.5 and 1.5. |
| `base_delay_ms` | non-negative integer | The unit the kind multiplies. Must be positive when any other backoff key is set. |
| `max_delay_ms` | positive integer | Ceiling on the computed delay. Unset means no practical ceiling. |

Both vocabularies are closed and checked at registration: a `kind` or `jitter`
value outside the list refuses the register as a hard error. There is no
silent fallback at retry time.

## Registration-time vocabulary checking

When a template registers, the runtime range-checks each `error_types` key
against the union of the vocabularies the key could legitimately come from:

- the error classes the node's executor advertises in its capabilities
  handshake,
- the runtime-synthesized classes, including everything under `acquire/`,
- the error classes advertised by every claim producer the node names.

A key attributable to none of those registers with a **warning**, never a
rejection. The warning names the executor, lists its declared classes, lists
the producers' declared classes, and says the policy will only match if a peer
emits that exact class. The register succeeds either way, so the warning is
the only signal you get — read the `validation_warnings` array in the register
response.

When no peer declares any vocabulary at all, there is nothing to check
against, and every key registers silently.

The check honours a trailing `/*` on the **declared** side. An executor that
advertises `agent/subprocess_exit/*` makes `agent/subprocess_exit/anything`
register without a warning. It does not make that key route anything other
than the exact class the executor emits.

## Where the class shows up

The class is the tail of the event kind. Filter the event log by the exact
kind string:

| Outcome | Event kind |
| --- | --- |
| Terminal failure (also emitted for `pass` and `give_up`) | `terminal/error/<class>` |
| In-place retry | `transient/retry/<n>/<class>`, where `n` is the retry counter |
| Release and requeue | `transient/release_and_requeue/<class>` |
| Dispatch fault outside the policy map | `transient/infra/<class>` |

The terminal-error event payload carries `error_class`, `error_payload`,
`attempt`, `retries_so_far`, `attributes_delta` and `tags`. The retry event
payload carries `error_class`, `attempt`, `cap`, `delay_ms` and
`error_payload`.

`GET /v1/events?kind=<kind>` accepts a full signal type-path as its `kind`
value and matches it **exactly**. `kind=terminal/error/http/network_error`
works; `kind=terminal/error/http` matches nothing. `instance_id`, `node_id`,
`since` and `until` narrow the same query.

## The vocabulary is per-deployment, not versioned

There is no global catalog of error classes and no version or deprecation
marker anywhere in the capabilities handshake. The classes a deployment
recognises are whatever its configured peers advertise at that moment, plus
the runtime-synthesized set. Two consequences:

- **Validity is per node, not global.** `agent/refused` registers clean on a
  node whose executor is the claude-agent executor and warns on a node whose
  executor is the http-node executor. `http/timeout` does the reverse.
- **Swapping an executor changes which classes are recognised**, and changes
  which of your `error_types` entries can ever fire. Re-read the register
  response's warnings after any change to a node's `executor` or
  `claim_producers` block.

Treat the class strings in this set as the vocabulary of *this* release's
bundled services and runtime. Nothing in the product promises them across an
upgrade.
